events.note: Authored by an AI agent run (issue #95, parent #92) from the cited language and format specifications and the provider support page, read on 2026-10-03, before any scanner output was consulted; synthetic values only; not independently reviewed.

Decided 2026-10-04 by the sole maintainer (Milo Kang, milocosmopolitan, repository owner), ADR 0019 item 3 (#95). This scenario states the policy its case projects. Question: When a separator (a literal line break, a Markdown line ending, a backslash-newline inside single quotes, an escaped newline text) interrupts a key-shaped value and nothing reconstructs it, must the fragments be protected? Options: A: protect the fragments (must-flag; the secret bytes are the fragments). B: the joined text is not a key (must-not-flag). C: decide per carrier; keep the three language-reconstruction cases as asserted. Decision: C, then A for the five separator cases (eight fixtures): a key-shaped value split by a separator is a partial leak and is protected; the secret bytes are the fragments and the separator bytes are not secret. The three language-reconstruction cases stay as they are (a fact question, tool-corroborated). The engine scores the enclosing range, so separator bytes count as secret until it scores fragments; the release notes say so. Reason: Half a key in clear text is still a leak, and a rule that protects only values a language rebuilds would let a separator launder a key. Project policy, not a provider rule or a fact. Finalized by the sole maintainer alone under the solo-maintainer period (ADR 0020): not reviewed, not independent validation, queued for retro-review (#154). Recorded by an AI agent on the owner's instruction.
events.dissent: No source says fragments must be protected; the case texts themselves say so. The provider documents the key as always 69 characters, so the joined text is not a documented key, and a rule that flags fragments turns ordinary wrapped prose with an SG. prefix into a must-flag input. Scoring the enclosing range counts separator bytes as secret, so a scanner that reports exactly the key characters can be marked partial.
events.reversingEvidence: A source stating that a separator-split value is not a key or is not to be protected, or an engine that scores fragments and shows the policy is unworkable (for example, a reliable false-positive report on wrapped prose).
